analysis.one_liner: Opens protected national forest roadless areas to road construction by canceling the 2001 Roadless Rule.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would wipe out the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule, has been referred to two committees and had a subcommittee hearing but has not reached a floor vote; it has 5 Republican sponsors and none from the other party.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2001, the government barred new road construction across roughly a third of America's national forest land — about 58 million acres — the largest such land-protection action in the country's history. This bill would declare that rule to have no force and permanently forbid any similar rule. It would then require the Forest Service to build roads for forest restoration, cutting back flammable brush and trees near communities and watersheds, and replacing or removing roads that damage forests. Since roadless rules keep timber harvesting, mining, and energy development out of those areas, canceling the rule would open them up.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passes, timber companies, mining companies, and energy developers gain road access into millions of acres of national forest where the 2001 rule has kept them out. Fire-prone communities near national forests could also benefit from the bill's mandated road-building for hazardous fuels reduction near homes and municipal watersheds.

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares the January 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (66 Fed. Reg. 3244) to have no force or effect, and bars the Agriculture Secretary from proposing, finalizing, or enforcing any rule substantially similar to it [S2].

It requires the Forest Service to construct permanent and temporary roads it deems necessary for restoration work, for hazardous fuels reduction in at-risk communities, the wildland-urban interface, and municipal watersheds, and to replace or decommission roads it finds harmful to forests or watersheds [S2].
The mandated road-building remains subject to environmental review requirements such as the National Environmental Policy Act [S2].

analysis.who_pays: If it passes, the public loses the protection now covering about 58 million acres of national forest — land that shelters fish and wildlife habitat and supplies drinking water to many downstream communities, since roads are a leading source of erosion and sediment in forest streams. Taxpayers bear the cost of building and maintaining the new roads the bill requires. Hunters, anglers, and other backcountry users lose the unroaded landscapes the rule protects.

drawbacks.text: Canceling the rule nationwide and permanently banning any similar rule goes far beyond the bill's stated fire-safety rationale: the rule covers roughly a third of all national forest land, not just areas near at-risk communities [S2].

Forest roads are a well-documented source of stream sediment and erosion, so a mandate to build roads in municipal watersheds cuts against the water-quality protections the rule was designed to provide for downstream towns [S2].

The bill requires the Agriculture Secretary to build roads, which means Congress is directing new taxpayer spending on construction and ongoing maintenance even as the Forest Service already carries a multi-billion-dollar road maintenance backlog.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The narrowest part of the bill — road access for fuels-reduction work near communities and municipal watersheds — has a real, though debated, purpose, and the bill keeps environmental review in place. But the main effect is sweeping: it voids the largest forest-land protection in U.S. history across its entire 58-million-acre footprint and permanently outlaws any replacement. The road-building mandates, which could be authorized in a far more targeted bill, function here as the justification for opening roadless areas generally to development.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late February 2026, referred to both the Agriculture and Natural Resources committees, sent to subcommittees, and got one subcommittee hearing in May — but no committee vote or floor action has followed, and the session runs into January 2027.

narrative.text: Rep. Harriet Hageman introduced the bill on February 25, 2026, with four original Republican cosponsors: Reps. Downing, Maloy, Stauber, and Tiffany [S2].
The Speaker referred it to the Agriculture Committee and, in addition, the Natural Resources Committee — a dual referral that gives two committees a claim on the bill [S4].
It was later referred to the Agriculture Subcommittee on Forestry and Horticulture and the Natural Resources Subcommittee on Federal Lands [S4].
A subcommittee hearing was held on May 21, 2026, but no markup, committee vote, or floor vote has occurred [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, the 2001 Roadless Rule remains in force, so backcountry users, downstream water users, and the timber and mining companies that were hoping for access are all still living under the status quo. The bill's sponsors have succeeded so far only in getting it heard at the subcommittee level.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Roadless forests stay protected for now

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors are Republicans — Hageman plus four of her 222 Republican colleagues — and no Democrat has signed on; no roll-call vote exists yet to show where the chambers split.

industries.note: Canceling the roadless rule lets logging companies build roads into roughly 58 million acres of national forest where harvesting has been barred. The public gives up protected watersheds and habitat to enable that access.

Roadless protections have kept hard-rock mining and oil and gas development out of unroaded forest; voiding the rule opens those areas to claims and exploration. The cost of new roads and lost protected land falls on the public.

Hunters, anglers, and quiet-recreation users lose unroaded backcountry if the rule is voided. The mandated fuels-reduction roads could lower fire risk for some communities, though roads themselves add erosion to the watersheds many towns depend on.

analysis.trajectory: With only five sponsors, dual committee referral, and no markup or vote nearly three months after a subcommittee hearing, this bill follows the path of most public-lands bills of this kind: it will likely sit in committee and expire at the end of the 119th Congress unless a committee chair chooses to advance it. Nullifying a 25-year-old rule that enjoys broad public support would also face a difficult floor vote even if it cleared committee.
